Description

Something went through the market square in the night and turned every stall out into the street. The town has gone quiet and shuttered. You have the keys, a pair of hands, and no one waiting on you. Put it all back.

Tidy Up the Town is a cosy first-person tidy-up game set in a medieval market square, and the things you tidy are a market's goods: bread, fish, cheese wheels, bottles, rings, hammers, tankards, chess pieces.

The sorting rule is the objects themselves. A fish goes to the fishmonger. A hammer goes to the smith. Nothing has to be learned, colour-coded or looked up - you already know the rule before the game starts. But the exact spot is yours to choose: an axe does not have one correct rack, it fits any weapon rack, and the first axe you put in one makes that rack the axe rack for the rest of the run.

There is no clock, no fail state, no customers to serve and nothing in the square that undoes your work. The mess is fixed at the start and only ever shrinks. Put the game down mid-armful and the square is exactly as tidy when you come back.

What you get for tidying is not a progress bar. Fill a stall and its merchant returns - unshutters, takes their place behind the counter, starts working. Fill their neighbours and the aisle between them picks up a customer at the bread, a child running through, a dog, a busker. Fill the square and it is a working market with the noise to match.

Key Features

  • Two verbs and nothing pushing back - pick a thing up, carry up to three, and take each to the stall it belongs to. No clock, no customers, no fail state, and nothing in the square that undoes your work.
  • The sorting rule is the goods themselves - hundreds of medieval market wares, each belonging to a trade you already know.
  • But the exact spot is yours to choose - the first axe you rack makes that rack the axe rack, and every other axe joins it, stacking neatly beside its fellows.
  • Fill a stall and its merchant comes home - the reward for tidying is the place becoming inhabited, at a rate you set.
  • Spells, not kit - unseen hands that carry for you, a longer reach, a gilt edge on every stray of the kind you are holding, and a pillar of light that catches whatever you throw into it. Every one buys efficiency, never power.
  • A market that keeps the real calendar - the square dresses itself for the season and the festival on the day it actually falls.
  • Stylised low-poly visuals at golden hour, built in Godot 4.
